item.title: Federal government holds American Samoa seabed mineral lease sale despite judge's ruling
item.description: The Marine Minerals Administration held a lease sale for offshore critical minerals near American Samoa, despite a federal judge’s ruling days earlier voiding the government’s environmental assessment. The administration said two areas covering 31.5 million acres of seabed near American Samoa were leased for $6 million.
item.content:encoded:
The Marine Minerals Administration held a lease sale for offshore critical minerals near American Samoa, despite a federal judge’s ruling days earlier voiding the government’s environmental assessment.

The administration said two areas covering 31.5 million acres of seabed near American Samoa were leased for $6 million.

Earthjustice, the environmental law firm that sued the federal government in the U.S. District Court of Hawaii, says it will pursue legal action to stop the leases.

“In deciding to move forward with today’s sale, the Trump administration has performed a renegade, unlawful act — a gambit that drew a single bidder offering the minimum price for the leases,” Earthjustice Ocean’s attorney Chris Eaton said in a news release. “We will use the full extent of the law to vigorously push for the leases to be voided. Deep-sea mining will cause unprecedented destruction to some of the ocean’s most pristine and unexplored reaches, and we will continue to fight for their protection.”

The case is being closely watched in the Marianas, where up to 69 million acres of seabed along both sides of the island chain are set to be leased on Dec. 16.

Last year, President Donald Trump ordered government agencies to fast-track seabed mineral exploration and extraction. He said critical minerals contained in polymetallic nodules found on the ocean floor are essential to U.S. economic and national security interests.

U.S. Interior Secretary Doug Burgum said the lease sale is delivering on Trump’s order.

“Critical minerals are used in everything from electronics to defense systems. A dependable critical minerals supply chain is essential to American manufacturing and the technologies that power our economy and national defense,” Burgum said. “Today’s sale opens a path to learn more about the resources off the coast of American Samoa and assess whether they could contribute to a more reliable domestic supply."

item.title: Sen. Christopher Dueñas selected as next legislative speaker
item.description: The Republican Party of Guam announced that Sen. Christopher Dueñas has been selected as the speaker of the 39 th Guam Legislature. Dueñas will continue to oversee the Office of Finance and Budget.
item.content:encoded:
The Republican Party of Guam announced that Sen. Christopher Dueñas has been selected as the speaker of the 39 th Guam Legislature.

Dueñas will continue to oversee the Office of Finance and Budget.

He said he looks forward to working with lawmakers from both parties to build a stronger, more prosperous Guam.

“Through the Office of Finance and Budget, I remain committed to responsible budgeting, fiscal discipline, and finally realizing the full implementation of performance-based budgeting, ensuring that government expenditures translate into measurable results for our people,” Dueñas said.

Sen. Telo Taitague will be vice speaker, and Shelly Calvo will be the legislative secretary.

Sen. Jesse Lujan will serve as majority leader, and Vincent Borja will be the majority whip.

Sen. Sabrina Salas-Matanane will chair the Committee on Rules.

The party said remaining committee chair assignments will be announced soon.

item.title: USS Frank Cable visits Saipan
item.description: The submarine tender USS Frank Cable visited Saipan over the weekend as part of an effort between CNMI leadership and Joint Region Marianas to bring more Navy ship visits to Saipan. Rear Adm. Brett Mietus said the people of the Northern Marianas have always welcomed Navy sailors like family, and the visit are good for the local economy.
item.content:encoded:
The submarine tender USS Frank Cable visited Saipan over the weekend as part of an effort between CNMI leadership and Joint Region Marianas to bring more Navy ship visits to Saipan.

Rear Adm. Brett Mietus said the people of the Northern Marianas have always welcomed Navy sailors like family, and the visit are good for the local economy.

“This visit is the result of listening to Commonwealth leaders and working together to make a great port visit,” Mietus said.

Port visits give sailors the chance to experience the culture of the CNMI, while bringing crew members into local restaurants, shops and attractions.

“We value our partnership with the CNMI, and we look forward to continuing our work so more of our ships and sailors can experience the commonwealth’s hospitality.”

During the visit Frank Cable sailors were scheduled to visit Gregorio T. Camacho Elementary School to assist with campus cleanup and beautification.

The visit reflects continued collaboration between the military and the Office of the Governor, Commonwealth Bureau of Military Affairs, Marianas Visitors Authority and Saipan Chamber of Commerce.

item.title: Paolo Bulgari, who turned a family jewelry business into a global brand, dies at 89
item.description: ATHENS, Greece (AP) — Paolo Bulgari, the grandson of a Greek silversmith who helped transform the family jewelry business into a global luxury brand synonymous with Italian glamour and design, has died. He was 89. His family announced his death Saturday, describing him as "the greatest jeweler of our time" and praising his humanity and entrepreneurial talent.
item.content:encoded:
ATHENS, Greece (AP) — Paolo Bulgari, the grandson of a Greek silversmith who helped transform the family jewelry business into a global luxury brand synonymous with Italian glamour and design, has died. He was 89.

His family announced his death Saturday, describing him as "the greatest jeweler of our time" and praising his humanity and entrepreneurial talent.

Bulgari presided for decades over a brand celebrated by supermodels, Hollywood stars and collectors for its bold designs and distinctive use of color.

Born in Rome in 1937, he was the grandson of Sotirios Voulgaris, who founded the jewelry business after leaving Greece. Originally from Paramythia, a mountain village in the Epirus region of northwestern Greece renowned for its silver jewelry, Voulgaris fled Ottoman rule and settled in Naples before opening a shop in Rome, adapting both his craft and his family name to his new home.

Paolo Bulgari joined the family business shortly after leaving school. Working alongside his father, Giorgio, he initially focused on precious stones, developing an expertise in gemstones that would inform his work as a designer and businessman throughout his career.

Turning away from the delicate aesthetic associated with Parisian jewelry houses, the Bulgari family embraced bold gemstones, rich yellow gold, generous proportions and unexpected combinations of color. Drawing inspiration from ancient Rome and Italy's artistic heritage, the distinctive style helped set the brand apart internationally.

Alongside his brother Nicola and nephew Francesco Trapani, Bulgari led the company's expansion into major luxury markets, opening stores in New York, Paris, Geneva and Monte Carlo. The business diversified beyond jewelry into watches, perfumes, leather goods and, eventually, hotels.

Heading the group since the mid-1980s, Bulgari guided the company through a period of significant international growth. Its jewelry was a fixture on celebrities spanning from Elizabeth Taylor to Zendaya. Tall and silver-haired, he occasionally appeared alongside the stars wearing his creations, maintaining a characteristically reserved presence.

In 2011, the family sold a controlling stake in the company to French luxury conglomerate LVMH in a deal valued at more than $5 billion, ending decades of direct family control.

Despite his association with the glamorous world of international luxury, Bulgari frequently referred to his family's humble start. In 2019, he and his wife established the Paolo Bulgari Foundation to support young people through schooling and job training in disadvantaged neighborhoods on the outskirts of Rome.

"Many people don't know it," he wrote in the foundation's introduction, "but at the origin of my surname there is a story of migration."

His funeral will be held Monday at the Basilica of Santa Croce in Rome.

item.title: Trump orders federal contractors to check with White House before responding to Congress
item.description: NEW YORK (AP) — President Donald Trump is directing federal contractors and subcontractors to consult with his administration about inquiries they receive from Congress and to withhold any communications that the White House considers privileged, according to a new executive order . The companies must also coordinate with the White House and U.S. agencies on "appropriate responses" to any such req
item.content:encoded:
NEW YORK (AP) — President Donald Trump is directing federal contractors and subcontractors to consult with his administration about inquiries they receive from Congress and to withhold any communications that the White House considers privileged, according to a new executive order .

The companies must also coordinate with the White House and U.S. agencies on "appropriate responses" to any such requests, the order issued late Friday says. If they fail to comply, the White House warns their contracts could be terminated and their future work with the federal government suspended.

The order is the Republican administration's latest effort to resist what are expected to be wide-ranging and aggressive oversight efforts from Democrats when they take over Congress in January. Democrats have made government contracts one of their top investigative targets , noting that federal money has been flowing to companies linked with Trump's family, particularly at the Pentagon.

White House officials have already begun taking steps to exert more control over how agencies and officials respond to congressional requests, anticipating there will be a flood of investigations initiated by Democrats.

Trump's counsel, Will Scharf, told federal agencies on Monday that they must seek approval from his office and the White House's Office of Legislative Affairs before agreeing to appear before Congress. Scharf also suggested in a recent letter to Rep. Robert Garcia of California, the top Democrat on the House Oversight Committee, that some congressional investigations may amount to "blatant criminality."

Garcia sent letters this week directing members of Trump's family and top administration officials to preserve documents. Scharf sought to dismiss the requests, noting in a letter to Democratic lawmakers that they are not yet in the majority and cannot compel compliance.

Responding to the new executive order, Garcia said it was part of the administration's "blatant attack on Congress' constitutional right to conduct oversight." He said that despite efforts to impede investigations, "we're just getting started."

In a fact sheet , the White House framed the new requirements as "protecting executive privileges from congressional overreach," arguing that some congressional leaders have tried to intrude on executive branch privileges by "harassing private companies that contract with the federal government."

Presidents of both parties have long used executive privilege to resist congressional inquiries, but the claims can set up messy, protracted legal fights as parties dispute whether it applies. Executive privilege allows the president to keep information from the courts, Congress and the public to protect the confidentiality of White House deliberations, but the protection is far from absolute.

The latest executive order applies to all contractors and subcontractors, a universe of tens of thousands of businesses.

item.title: Bayer reaches Roundup settlement that could cost the company billions
item.description: The agrochemical and biotech giant Bayer has agreed to pay billions of dollars to people who sued the company alleging the weed-killer Roundup caused their cancer. On Friday, a judge in Missouri gave final approval to the nationwide settlement that could cost the company up to $7.25 billion in the coming years.
item.content:encoded:
The agrochemical and biotech giant Bayer has agreed to pay billions of dollars to people who sued the company alleging the weed-killer Roundup caused their cancer.

On Friday, a judge in Missouri gave final approval to the nationwide settlement that could cost the company up to $7.25 billion in the coming years.

The money will go to thousands of people who have been or will be diagnosed with non-Hodgkin lymphoma — a blood cancer that they claim is linked to glyphosate, which is the main ingredient in Roundup.

Under the settlement in circuit court, people affected could receive anywhere from $10,000 to $165,000 in compensation, depending on whether their work in agriculture or other occupations exposed them to higher levels of glyphosate, the age when they were diagnosed with non-Hodgkin lymphoma and other factors.

In a statement , the CEO of Bayer, Bill Anderson, called the settlement a "decisive milestone" that will "mitigate the risks" of pending and future litigation.

The presiding judge, Timothy Boyer, said it was "among the largest in the history of mass tort personal-injury class action settlements."

Earlier this year, the U.S. Supreme Court ruled in favor of Bayer, the German company that now owns Monsanto, finding that it could be shielded from lawsuits filed in state courts over claims that it failed to warn consumers about the cancer-causing effects of glyphosate.

Roundup is the most widely used weed-killer in the world.

The attorney representing the plaintiffs, Christopher Seeger, said in a statement that "Today's final approval order delivers guaranteed compensation to Roundup cancer victims who have waited more than a decade for justice."

The latest settlement comes in addition to a previous one in which Bayer agreed to pay between about $10 billion and $11 billion to settle more than 100,000 claims related to Roundup.

More than a decade ago, the World Health Organization's cancer agency concluded that glyphosate is probably carcinogenic to humans. Prominent scientists in the field of environmental health have echoed those concerns as recently as this year.

But Bayer has steadfastly denied that its product causes cancer.

The Environmental Protection Agency has also concluded it "did not identify risks of concern from glyphosate uses, including for cancer," though the agency is currently conducting a review of the evidence related to human health after facing intense pressure from advocates and some scientists.

Concerns about the safety of glyphosate has been an animating issue for supporters of Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr and his Make America Healthy Again agenda.

However, the Trump administration has taken steps to support the herbicide-maker, siding with Bayer in the Supreme Court case and issuing an executive order to promote domestic production of glyphosate.

Several years ago, the company removed glyphosate from its U.S. products used in residential settings, although it's still in use in the agricultural industry.

item.title: Storms expected on both coasts threatens Thanksgiving travel
item.description: Before worrying about the temperature of the turkey, travelers could face a different type of uncertainty next week. This time , it's the weather — and it's affecting both U.S. coasts. "I know there's a lot of travel for many of you as you head into the Thanksgiving holiday, but I'm going to ask you all to consider not traveling unless it is absolutely essential," said San Francisco Mayor Daniel L
item.content:encoded:
Before worrying about the temperature of the turkey, travelers could face a different type of uncertainty next week. This time , it's the weather — and it's affecting both U.S. coasts.

"I know there's a lot of travel for many of you as you head into the Thanksgiving holiday, but I'm going to ask you all to consider not traveling unless it is absolutely essential," said San Francisco Mayor Daniel Lurie on X Friday . He said the city is preparing this weekend for extreme high tides and rain that could hit the area Monday afternoon through Wednesday.

Over the past week, cities in California saw mudslides, waterspouts and flooding while Florida also saw coastal flooding and inundated streets. A new set of storms are expected to hit both sides of the country early next week, just as travelers head into the holiday week.

It's already been a wet fall in large swaths of the country, thanks in part to a Super El Niño , a natural climate pattern that shifts weather around the world. Devastating flooding in the Southwest U.S. left multiple people dead and hundreds stranded, and California and the Pacific Northwest have seen high sea level and multiple strong atmospheric rivers .

"Take this weekend: get yourself ready," Lurie, the San Francisco mayor, said after a call with the National Weather Service and the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.

Rain and snow, in higher elevations, is possible over parts of the northwest and northern California on Saturday, according to the NWS .

The West Coast is forecasted to see an atmospheric river, a narrow band of water vapor pushed by the wind, on Monday. Another is expected for the Pacific Northwest later in the week, according to the Center for Western Weather and Water Extremes . Atmospheric rivers hang over an area and dump precipitation. They can cause months worth of rain in just a few days.

The center expects two to four inches of precipitation over northern California and southern Oregon through Wednesday.

Coastal flood advisories are also in effect through Monday morning in the Bay Area, the NWS said. This comes on top of historic high tides , known as King tides.

A storm that started in Florida Friday will move north to the Mid-Atlantic and into the Northeast by Sunday evening, according to the NWS .

Some of the heaviest rain could be seen on the coast of the Carolinas through Sunday morning. Then, heavy rain is expected to move up the coast, said Dan Hoffman, a meteorologist at the National Weather Service in Baltimore, Md.

Hoffman said during a busy travel week, even with the weather not expected to bring flooding or strong winds, it "doesn't usually take too much to cause things to start to have delays."

As for New England, Andrew Loconto, a meteorologist at the NWS in Norton, Mass., said the storm this weekend is not forecasted to be as big as another storm hitting the region after Thanksgiving. "That could be more impacts for people coming back home," Loconto said, pointing to another highly anticipated day across the U.S. — Black Friday.
